newsitem.title: UK: Bass chairman sees buoyant UK consumer spending.
newsitem.headline: Bass chairman sees buoyant UK consumer spending.

text.p: Sir Ian Prosser, chairman of brewer to leisure group Bass Plc, said on Wednesday the company expected continued buoyancy in UK consumer spending over the next year.

"Bass Taverns' investment programme will take advantage of this healthy economic background. We expect restored growth in our leisure business and in a competitive beer market Bass Brewers will consolidate its new product growth," said Prosser in a statement.

The company said it planned to spend 670 million stg on the business during the year to September 30, 1997 of which 300 million stg will go on its Bass Taverns to create more branded pubs like Irish pubs O'Neils and finding new sites for its Harvester pub-restaurants.

The 300 million invested in Bass Taverns will take advantage of "buoyancy" the company expects in UK consumer spending over the next year, said Prosser in an interview shortly after the company announced its results.

Prosser said he thought consumer expenditure had grown around three percent this year and with various tax changes and the growing consumer confidence, "I would expect that to continue or be slightly higher next year."
He said the hotel business, where Holiday Inn improved trading profits by 18.9 percent to 195 million stg, continued to offer good prospects.

Bass will spend 100 million, of the total 670 million set aside for next year, on its Holiday Inns business, refurbishing existing hotels or taking small equity stakes in hotels it converts for outside parties.
In America, revenue per available room (revpar) was up 5.6 percent for managed hotels and 5.9 percent for franchised ones. In Europe, Africa and the Middle East revpar was up 8.5 percent.

The company added 280 hotels during the year. At the year end, it had some 2,249 hotels and 387,000 roooms. It also had franchise agreements for 559 hotels which had yet to join the Holiday Inn system.
Bass has earmarked 120 million stg of the 670 million for developing its leisure division, which includes 45 million to replace amusement machines.

Amusement machines performance improved from the previous year's low showing, with total income up by 8.1 percent. The company is expected to benefit from changes in the law last June allowing 10 pound all cash machines in pubs and letting amusement machines into betting offices.
It will spend spend 100 million on Bass Brewers, including overseas brewing and 50 million on Britvic, said Prosser.

Brewing profits increased nine percent to 157 million in the year although Prosser said conditions remained competitive in beer in both sales to supermarkets and pubs. "Our sucess this year in brewing has been because of new product innovation."

Cream ale Caffrey's, launched three years ago, sold 270,000 barrels in 1995, rising to 420,000 barrels in 1996. "Alcopop" Hoopers Hooch sold 320,000 barrels in 1996 and continues to have "very good prospects" despite a 46 percent hike in tax imposed on alcopops in the UK budget.
"There is no objective evidence at all that says underage people are seduced by Hoopers Hooch," said Prosser.
The company's Britvic soft drinks division saw profits grow 8.7 percent to 50 million in the year pushed ahead by its acquisition of the Robinsons brand in 1995.
